A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RTop-K research, despite the revised title and presentation. All pages, algorithms, tables, figures, and references are readable. v1 has no appendix; v3's Appendices A and B are included in this comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original iteration-count and approximation simulations, GPU timing measurements, and GraphSAGE training speed and accuracy results in Tables 1–4 and Figures 4–5.

after.justification: v3 reports original kernel benchmarks and GraphSAGE, GCN, and GIN experiments, alongside additional iteration-count, vector-size, and precision analyses in its appendices.

M1.justification: The binary-search method and one-warp-per-vector GPU design remain. However, Algorithm 1 changes threshold initialization, termination, and borderline-element collection. Algorithm 2 removes the cnt=k break and updates the lower threshold when cnt>=k, executing the prescribed iteration count. These are localized procedural revisions, not merely renamed variables.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate row-wise top-k selection and MaxK-GNN training/testing on Flickr, Yelp, Reddit, and ogbn-products. Adding GCN/GIN configurations and varying vector dimensions extends experimental settings without adding datasets, domains, or distinct tasks.

E2.justification: PyTorch remains the evaluated kernel comparator, and optimal top-k remains the accuracy reference in the GNN experiments. GCN and GIN are additional application models, not competing selection methods. The related-work discussion does not establish additional evaluated top-k baselines.

E3.justification: The reported compiler changes from NVCC 12.2 to 12.6, and the main no-early-stopping precision changes from 10^-4 to 10^-16. v3 adds GCN/GIN evaluations and appendix protocols spanning vector sizes up to 8192, k up to 512, and multiple precision settings, with N=65536 in Figures 6–7. These substantially broaden the experimental configurations.

E4.justification: v3 expands early-stopping sensitivity tests beyond GraphSAGE to GCN and GIN. Appendix A compares predicted and measured iteration counts, while Appendix B adds vector-size scaling and precision sensitivity analyses. These investigate convergence, the limits of acceleration, and whether precision materially affects runtime.

E5.justification: New Table 5 specifies 10^4 repetitions per (M,k) configuration for the epsilon=0 analysis. The original analyses retain their 10^5 repetitions, so this is additional repetition information for a separate experiment, not a reduction of the original run counts. Neither version reports confidence intervals or run-to-run uncertainty for kernel timing or GNN accuracy.

E6.justification: Table 3 replaces average early-stopping speedups of 4.245–9.506x with 7.99–11.49x, and the no-early-stopping value changes from 3.936x to 7.29x. These are results under revised settings, not controlled same-setting gains. Table 4 revises GraphSAGE scores, including ogbn-products from 80.59% to 80.08%, and adds GCN/GIN results. The appendices add substantial scaling and convergence results; Tables 1–2 retain their numerical entries.

T1.justification: v1 provides empirical convergence and approximation statistics without the later derivations. Appendix A introduces a Gaussian assumption and derives an approximate expected iteration count using threshold quantiles, element spacing, and the initial search range. Appendix B adds an O(M log M) complexity argument and comparison with RadixSelect's O(M) scaling. These are substantial new mathematical analyses, although not proofs of neural-network accuracy preservation.

C1.justification: The central contribution remains GPU row-wise binary-search top-k with optional approximation and limited accuracy impact. v3 adds the GPU-algorithm survey and performance-limit analysis as an explicit contribution. Its abstract and conclusion replace the headline speedup claims and emphasize quantified MaxK-GNN training acceleration of 11.97%–33.29%, refining the earlier broader training/inference framing.

C2.justification: Appendix B adds substantive applicability limits: the no-early-stopping version becomes slower than PyTorch for large tested vectors, and the current shared-memory strategy cannot directly handle M>8192. It also explains scaling through memory behavior and RadixSelect overhead. Appendix A discusses approximation bias, while Section 4.3 qualifies the accuracy interpretation with the GIN-on-Flickr exception.

D1.justification: v3 replaces the anonymous implementation link with a named GitHub repository. It newly specifies N=#Nodes, M=256, and k=32 for the model experiments and discloses the A6000 allocation of floor(8192/M) warps per block. These improve access and implementation documentation without establishing a new warp-allocation method.

R1.justification: v3 adds references for SBP, the evaluated GNN architectures, and graph datasets, while removing several introductory GNN-application references and updating the supercomputer source. It identifies PyTorch's underlying method as RadixSelect. The central positioning against methods optimized for small batches of long vectors remains.

P1.justification: The overall introduction–related work–framework–experiments–conclusion sequence is retained. v3 revises the title and abstract, condenses algorithm background, expands threshold and GPU explanations, and splits the former Result Analytics subsection into kernel and model evaluations. These are localized narrative revisions alongside the new scientific material.

P2.justification: v3 changes to a predominantly single-column conference layout with wrapped algorithms and figures. The matched kernel figure changes from 21 to 12 panels, while the GNN figure expands from four to twelve panels; their numbering is exchanged. Tables 3–4 gain dimension/model breakdowns, and Table 5 and Figures 6–7 are added. Existing diagrams are also resized, relocated, or relabeled.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens evidence about applicability beyond v1's GraphSAGE-only evaluation and short-vector benchmarks. Additional GNN tests, iteration-model comparisons, and precision/size analyses reveal both useful operating regimes and concrete performance and memory limits. These address important gaps in validation and scope. The analysis remains approximate, timing/accuracy uncertainty is absent, and retained Tables 1–2 are not explicitly reconciled with the revised pseudocode. Nevertheless, the expanded validation and candid applicability boundaries provide a substantial net improvement; larger headline speedups alone do not establish it.
